hints: Compare the solid line (without CO) to the dashed line (with CO) in each graph. Look carefully at two places: how steep the start is at low partial pressure of oxygen, and how high the curve plateaus at high partial pressure.
Remember carbon monoxide has two effects: it blocks haem groups so they cannot carry oxygen, and it makes the remaining haem groups hold onto oxygen more tightly.
walkthrough:
**Recall the normal curve**

Think of the solid line first. Without carbon monoxide, haemoglobin shows its normal sigmoid (S-shaped) dissociation curve. Saturation starts low, rises steeply, then levels off near 100% at high partial pressure of oxygen.

**Apply what carbon monoxide does**

Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin with very high affinity to form carboxyhaemoglobin. This does two things. First, those haem groups are blocked, so maximum oxygen saturation can never reach 100%. Second, it increases the oxygen affinity of the remaining haem groups, so the curve shifts to the left at low partial pressures.

**Match to the graphs**

We need a dashed line that is steeper on the left (left shift) but plateaus much lower than the solid line. Only graph A shows both features: the dashed line rises faster at first, crosses the solid line, then flattens at about 40-50% saturation.

options.A: Correct. The dashed line rises more steeply at low pO2 (left shift, higher affinity) but plateaus far below 100% because CO has permanently blocked many oxygen binding sites.
options.B: Shows a left shift but the dashed line still reaches almost 100% saturation. This forgets that CO-blocked haem cannot carry oxygen, so maximum saturation must fall.
options.C: Shows a shift to the right with almost the same maximum. A right shift is the Bohr effect (due to CO2, H+ ions, low pH), not the effect of carbon monoxide.
options.D: Shows oxygen saturation becoming much higher with CO present. This is impossible because CO reduces oxygen transport by occupying binding sites.
